say.text: A 35-year-old has 30% scald burns. Six hours on, his pulse is 120 and his BP is 90/60. Urine output is low, and his haematocrit has risen from 42 to 52.
What type of shock is this?

choices.label: Septic: an infected burn driving the shock
Hypovolaemic: plasma leaking out of the vessels
Cardiogenic: the heart failing as a pump
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the haematocrit first. What would make it climb this early, before any infection has had time to act?
Not septic. A haematocrit rising from 42 to 52 means plasma is leaving the vessels, which is the burn leak, not infection.
It is tempting because burns do get infected, and he is tachycardic and hypotensive. But in the first hours the plasma leak comes first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the model: burn shock is plasma loss first.

say.text: Not cardiogenic. The clue is the haematocrit, which is climbing. That points to plasma loss, not a pump that has failed.
It is tempting because burn shock does involve some myocardial depression. But that is the second contributor, not the main cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the heart is a second contributor. The main problem is plasma loss.

say.text: Local burns release mediators that open capillaries. A large burn, above about 30%, leaks plasma even from uninjured skin. The heart is affected too, but the first loss is volume.
Yes. Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, with some myocardial depression added by circulating mediators. The rising haematocrit is your clue to plasma loss.
The heart is somewhat depressed too, so the pump can look like the problem.
In the first 24 hours, what is the first-line treatment?

choices.label: Titrated Ringer lactate, adjusted to the response
Albumin infusion started at once, alongside crystalloid
Inotropes to support the heart's pumping strength
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the burn is losing, not what is struggling to pump. Which fluid replaces that loss first?
Not at once. Classic Parkland gives crystalloid alone in the first 24 hours, so albumin does not start now.
It is tempting because colloid sits in the Evans and Brooke formulae. Colloid waits until the capillary leak settles, about 8 to 24 hours.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the rule: no colloid in the first 24 hours of classic Parkland.

say.text: Not inotropes. Pushing the heart harder does not replace the plasma that has leaked out.
It is tempting because the myocardium is depressed. But that is the second contributor, so the first move is fluid.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order: plasma first, then the heart.

say.text: Yes. Ringer lactate is the fluid of choice. In classic Parkland no colloid goes in during the first 24 hours.
A forearm scald looks mottled red and white. It hurts less than the skin around it, and the capillary refill is sluggish.
What depth is this burn?

choices.label: Full thickness (third degree), since it hurts least
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Less pain is not the same as no pain. Look at the colour of the burn and how fast the skin refills.
Not full thickness. Full-thickness skin is painless and leathery, but this burn is only less painful, and it still refills slowly.
It is tempting because pain seems to fall in a straight line with depth, so the least painful burn looks deepest. Less pain is a clue, not a grade.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the signs: pain alone does not grade depth. Colour, blanching and refill do.

say.text: Full thickness is painless, but a deep partial burn is only less painful. Pain sits on a spectrum, so it cannot grade depth on its own.
Read colour, blanching and refill, and expect the true depth to show over 48 to 72 hours.
Yes. Deep partial thickness is mottled, less painful and slow to refill. It can take more than 3 weeks to heal, with scarring, and often needs grafting.
Two burns look alike at first glance. Which feature separates full thickness from deep partial thickness?

choices.label: Less painful than normal skin, with slow refill
Heals in over 3 weeks, leaving scarring
Dry, leathery, insensate, and does not blanch
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the skin is still doing. Does it still feel a pin, and does it still blanch?
Not this one. Less pain with slow refill is the deep partial picture, so it cannot separate the two.
It is tempting because you have just used it to grade a burn. But full thickness is recognised by being insensate.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the rule: reduced pain belongs to deep partial. Full thickness is insensate.

say.text: Not this one. Healing over 3 weeks with scarring is a deep partial feature, and full thickness needs excision and grafting instead.
It is tempting because scarring looks like a severe burn. But the test is how the skin looks and feels, not how long it takes to heal.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix it: healing time belongs to deep partial. Full thickness is judged by look and feel.

say.text: Yes. Full thickness is dry, leathery and insensate, and it does not blanch. Reduced pain alone never grades depth.
One rule before the fluid sums: simple erythema is not counted in total body surface area (TBSA).
